prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a coarse layout of a compact gym: the floor spans the middle distance, a bench lies roughly 1–2 m in front and slightly right, nearby equipment and weights sit along the left and rear edges, and another person remains about 1–2 m ahead, mostly in the upper-right part of each view. Brighter regions indicate that the person, bench ends, yellow floor object, and finally the camera wearer’s forearms are nearer than the dark floor and background equipment; in frame 5 the forearms are within arm’s reach, approximately 0.2–0.6 m away, and occlude much of the right foreground. Across the frames, head rotation shifts the bench and person laterally through the view, while the person stays at a broadly similar distance and turns from a side-on orientation toward a more frontal/oblique one without clear evidence of looking directly at the camera. This map makes front-to-back separation and near-object occlusion clearer than RGB, but its smooth gradients, bright boundary halos, clipped objects, and unknown metric scale make metre estimates and distances between similarly shaded objects unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map separates several foreground regions from the otherwise black scene, most consistently marking the other person about 1–2 m ahead and above the bench in image coordinates, while also isolating scattered equipment regions to the left, center, and right. It shows that the person is partly cut off by the top edge throughout, that objects near the side boundaries are only partially visible, and that the camera wearer’s near arms/hands occupy and occlude the right foreground in frame 5; however, most benches, weights, and floor structures are entirely unmasked. The person’s mask moves from right-of-center toward the center and back toward the right as the viewpoint turns, but mask shape alone gives only weak evidence of facing direction and cannot determine gaze; no reliable object-to-person reach relation is available beyond the near foreground being within roughly 0.5 m of the camera wearer. Instance boundaries reveal silhouettes and overlap more clearly than RGB, but labels such as “suitcase,” “keyboard,” “sink,” and “bicycle,” the fragmented final-frame masks, and the missing gym equipment are visibly unreliable, so their identities and metric distances should not be trusted.
descriptions.pose: The pose map provides sparse articulated geometry: magenta hand detections appear in frames 1–2, a larger yellow body/arm skeleton appears around frame 2, and a short yellow limb chain appears in frame 3, while frames 4–5 contain no dependable skeletons. Where detected, the joints clarify relative positions—hands below and left of the other person’s upper body and connected limbs extending diagonally—but they do not recover the bench, floor, surrounding equipment, or enough torso/head landmarks to establish gaze or a stable facing direction. The detections suggest lateral viewpoint change and changing limb projection across the first three frames, yet they are too discontinuous to distinguish approach or retreat or to estimate distances beyond the RGB-based roughly 1–2 m separation from the other person; the camera wearer’s frame-5 hands, clearly within about 0.2–0.6 m, are missed. The skeleton overlay makes limb articulation easier to see than RGB where it exists, but severe missing joints, likely false or mismatched hand detections, edge truncation, and total dropout in later frames make reach, occlusion, and temporal motion judgments unreliable.
